بَاذِخٌ High, or lofty; (JK, A, Msb;) applied to a mountain: (JK, Msb:) [and] a high, or lofty, mountain; an epithet in which the quality of a subst. is predominant: (L, TA:) pl. بَوَاذِخُ (JK, S, A, L, Msb) and بَاذِخَاتٌ [both fem. forms]: (JK:) and the former pl. applied as an epithet to mountains. (S, A, K.) ―
-b2- [Hence,] رَجُلٌ بَاذِخٌ, (JK, L,) and ↓ بَذَّاخٌ , (JK, A, L,) [the latter an intensive epithet,] (tropical:) A proud, and lofty, or haughty, man, who exalts himself above others, (JK, A, L,) by his speech, and his glorying, or boasting: (JK, L:) pl. of the former بُذَخَآءُ, like as عُلَمَآءُ is pl. of عَالِمٌ, and بُذَّخٌ. (L.) You say, In speech, he is ↓ بَذَّاخٌ ; and in poetry, بَاذِخٌ. (L.) ―
-b3- And شَرَفٌ بَاذِخٌ (tropical:) High, or exalted, nobility. (S, K, TA.) ―
-b4- بَعِيرٌ بَاذِخٌ, (L,) and ↓ بَذَّاخٌ , (L, K,) or الهَدِيرِ ↓ بَذَّاخُ , (A,) and ↓ بِذْخٌ , and ↓ بَذِخٌ , (K,) (tropical:) A camel that brays much, (K,) or in the most vehement manner, (L,) and puts forth his شِقْشِقَة [or faucial bag]. (K.)
From An Arabic-English Lexicon (Edward William Lane)
